Like, especially given again the continuity and, you know, the fact that your guys >> No, it's good. Uh, I mean, in the NFL and college is different. You know, college is where everybody like you might leave with your peoples, you know, outside of the facility, but like in the NFL like everybody go home. So like in the facility it's it is our home you know away from college type. So like uh man we're close our our room is uh close you know uh we laugh you know and nothing that we say you know we troll a lot you know we troll a lot so uh nobody takes it to heart especially you know with me I I can't hold back you know what I say. So uh everybody already knows it though that you know I love to laugh so you know when I troll everybody just be like you know brush it off but they laugh. So, you know, uh feel like we got a good room. Nobody takes nothing to heart and everybody's very coachable, you know. Uh say if I say something to AJ, he'll be like, "Yeah, you're right." You know, and that's crazy, you feel me? Cuz I'm year four, he going to year eight, I think. So, it's like, man, uh that that shows how how our room is. >> Appreciate it. >> It was good. It was um pretty short compared to others, but it's so good to be back. I feel like uh you know, we coming right in where we left off at. Um playing at a high level, good chemistry. Um it's just so good to have all the guys back. Um and when you have everybody here, you just could feel, you know, the momentum that we had uh from last year and even the new additions are coming in with the same mentality. So, yeah, it's been fun. >> What's the potential for your secondary with the addition of Kevin? I I feel like, you know, like coach always say stay away from predictions and stuff, but I just wanted to say that the confidence is high. Like it's really high. Um and uh I want us to be the strength of the defense. >> What does he bring to your defense? What skills does he help? Um he he brings what every great safety would bring to a defense is uh communication, knowledge, experience, um ball skills, like you can name it, he he he's done it. He's uh played this long and at a high level for so long. Um and he's showing it right now in practice and meeting rooms and uh just giving us all a little bit more confidence back there. Um knowing that, you know, he's back there and that he's orchestrating the show. One of the things that uh coach Rabel said about you, your ability to play at a continuously high level for such a long time was you've been able to add some stuff to your game over the years. >> Oh, for sure. Yeah. Hell yeah. Like I couldn't be I wouldn't play at this level for this long if I wasn't continuing to add things and continuing to be like a student of the game. Um you know, from the knowledge standpoint, from just going back over the basics and remastering the basics. um never getting too old with the the uh the things that seem simple but also uh you know play a huge role and uh you know technique and being closer to the ball and you know just uh the proximity to the ball. So yeah, I just you know hone in on being a student and trying to learn every day. >> One of the things that he said was he kind of compared you to a baseball pitcher. Are you a baseball guy in terms of like you know you you learn things as you get older and you kind of pick up wisdom over the course of your >> Yeah. Oh, for sure. Uh that's definitely what's going on. and even like playing in different schemes, different defenses, uh playing in NFC, AFC, uh having success and uh even having like you know the losses, it's it's all a learning experience for me. Um, like one thing coach say is, uh, don't take yourself too serious. And when he says that, it speaks to the ego and it speaks to, you know, me not having a big ego and being able to learn from anybody, coach, player, um, learning from the film and, uh, you know, even though you play this longer, you have had some success, you still, you know, come in there like a rookie, still really curious about, you know, what you can know more. >> You look back at last season in the defense accomplishments and room for growth, what do you, what do you see? what's the foundation that you laid and what needs to get better uh coming season? Uh, I feel like, you know, as a defense, we laid a foundation of just being like, I don't know, like showstoppers, like, you know what I'm saying? Like, we played great ball, especially towards the end. It was like lights out. Um, you know, and we also picked up our ball production in the playoffs, which we wanted to do during the season, which we, you know, kind of want to get into during the season is picking up our ball production and, uh, just being more stout, better in the red zone for sure. Um, playing better defense down there. Obviously, we don't want to have too many trips down there, but when we do get down there, we want to uh deny them touchdowns and make them kick field goals. >> AJ Brown on the team and just what's made him such a productive receiver? >> Uh, I mean, he's just a big body, great control, um, good knowledge for the game. Um, you know, he's he's a great guy to go up against every day to hone your skills in on. Um, and I've played him before, but you know, it's going to be great work playing against him every day. And, you know, also him going up against us, it's going to be uh, better for both sides. >> How's your guy Gunzel look this summer? How you how's your guy Gonzo look? >> He's good. He's uh he's Gonzo. I mean like Gonzo's being Gonzo. Um something that we all expected and um you know we happy to have him back. >> Carl, how important is it to basically forget about last year and realize that this is a new year, new team, and the process starts now to accomplish what you want to accomplish for this year's team. >> Oh, it was easy. That been like I would say like in March it was already like a reset. I don't think anybody has come in here expecting success without putting in the work. That's just not how this team is built from the top down from our coach down to the players down to the co the training staffs and even like the gas like everybody knows that we have to build our way back up and uh you can feel it. I've been on teams and you know you play good one year the next year it's kind of like well we'll get there we'll get there. No, we're we want to get there now. We want to start training now. Um and you can tell that's the vibes around here. >> All right. Thanks. >> Appreciate it. Thank you. >> Thank you.

title: New England Patriots Offensive Assistants Address the Media | Patriots Press Conference
text: First off, just what's the orientation process been like for AJ? >> Uh, it's been pretty smooth. You know, he obviously uh loves football, football junkie, so he spends a lot of time uh, you know, with me and with other coaches and with Drake trying to learn the system. He's been doing a great job. >> What does that look like just inside the room when you have a veteran presence walk in like that? >> Uh, I think, you know, he commands respect with what he's done in this league. Um, but we got a a really good room and welcoming room. Uh, so they were happy to have him and he's been getting along with the guys great and they've been helping him out and so it's been a good process. >> Todd, what do you remember him being as a rookie in 2019? I know you were the tight ends, coach them, but you know, just remember watching him grow as a rookie and to the point when you were the became the offensive coordinator. >> Yeah, you could see his competitive spirit and his love for the game uh pretty early. I would say that uh he was a little bit raw in terms of uh understanding some of the you know specifics of schematics and why we did certain things but uh quickly learned he had a great receiver coach and Rob Moore um who I've known for a long time and Rob really did a great job of bringing him along is understanding the why behind things and I think that's something that helped accelerate his growth by the time I became the coordinator. you know, we brought in Julio Jones and Julio played the X position. So AJ had to move over to Z and uh handled that very well and you know, handled all the concepts very well um to boot. So yeah, he did a great job of growing up there and is even more grown now. >> What does his leadership style look like? He was talking last week about having to earn it in front of the group. >> He starts with accountability. Um you know, tell you a quick story. his first practice or I guess it was his second practice. Uh he had a drop on a go ball and after practice wanted to do push-ups for the the drop in front of the group and everybody chose to uh do it together. So creating and augmenting that uh culture of mutual accountability I think it's been awesome. >> Todd, you guys brought back a lot of guys, patted some guys. How big of a factor is competition going to be with this group? >> Competition is always great. I think it brings the best out of true competitors. Um, I'm really fortunate because I have a room of good football players but really good men. Uh, and so they're, you know, supporting each other, uh, but also finding a way to to keep that competition something that drives them. So, I'm really pleased with where the culture of the room is right now and and, uh, I'm fortunate to coach the guys that do. >> How automatic has the chemistry kind of become between like AJ and Drake as well as Romeo, the new guys? >> I think when you're like-minded and in purpose and how you approach things, it's easy to get along. Uh, and those are definitely guys that we've added with Romeo and AJ, uh, that kind of fit how we want to do things around here, you know, and I think that having some knowledge of who AJ was before he got here helps us know that he's going to integrate quickly and, um, you know, that that's been great to watch. >> Does that knowledge of working with AJ before help you maybe with Josh a little bit in terms of, you know, what's like to call plays with him out there? I've certainly had some conversations with Josh about things that I know are are right up AJ's alley and in his skill set. Um, I would say that we're pretty early in the process of of what that would look like uh in terms of game planning or anything like that. So, uh, you know, I'm sure those conversations will come more and more as as AJ gets more and more comfortable. >> With Kan not here for OTAs, how are you just going about the the process of bringing him back into the mix this week? >> Well, obviously he knew the system. you know, being here last year, it was pretty quick to catch him up on any tweaks that that we had or anything that changed. He had a great day yesterday. Really good to see him in shape and and doing the things he was doing full speed yesterday. So, excited where he's at. Excited to have him back. >> When you guys are evaluating the back end of the depth chart at wide receiver, how important is it for a guy to have special teams experience and how much does that figure into his overall chances of making the team? I think back end of the depth chart or the front end of the depth chart, you should be looking for every way you can to help the team. Um certainly availability is is one of the best abilities you can have and guys that know what to do and how to do it on special teams, they usually find a way to get a jersey, you know, so um obviously a very talented room, but I think from top to bottom, those guys should be looking at how they can help in any phase. >> Todd, back at the combine, I think it was Mike talked about how big year one to year two is at the receiver position to make a jump. What have you seen from Kyle specifically this spring that could allow him to to do that? >> Some of those little details, the route tops, the play strength, um, you know, proper footwork, uh, who he has in the run game, blocking force, all those things I think are a little bit cleaner to him. The picture is a little bit slower to him than it was last year. Really pleased with where he's at. He's been working his tail off. Uh, he's moving all over the place, handling a big role. So, uh, very pleased with where K's at. When you're in the system, it's all about learning what to do, you know, and and how do you fit in the system and then as you continue to grow through the system, it's okay, how do I operate this at a high level, you know, and so I think we're trying to weaponize Drake's mind and all the quarterback's mind as opposed to just being, you know, throwers of the football. We want to be operators of the offense. >> There were a couple plays yesterday, Ashton, where >> you guys hurried to the line. >> Yeah. >> But then didn't hurry to snap it. here. Is that an example maybe of what you're talking about where he's able to kind of maybe assess and adjust if there I think that's a cool tool that we talked about coach Vable and coach McDaniels in the offseason where you know let's just go on the ball and not give Drake a play and let him practice solving the problems himself. Uh, so sometimes there'll be a play called with some of the uptempo stuff and then other times it's just, hey, on the ball, here's a formation and you figure it out. And so then we can go into the meeting room and kind of talk about what he was thinking, why he was thinking. If it was a great answer, you give him a pat on the back. And if it's something we might want to tweak or adjust, we talk about it. But it's easy to say solve the problems, but if you never let him practice solving problems, then you know, you're just talking to a cement wall. So we're giving him opportunities to go out there and do those things. >> Does that happen in a game? Um, we'll see, you know, if how it looks or something, and that happens from time to time. And, you know, some quarterbacks around the league run the two-minute drill by themselves. Um, and I'm not saying that's something that we're going to do or not do. We'll have those conversations at a later date. Um, but I mean, we're prepared for it and preparing for it in case we ever have to use that tool. >> Did you handle it okay yesterday? >> Yeah, I think he did a good job. >> Hats on the back. >> Yeah, pats on the back for sure. >> So, you said that was a brainchild of Josh and Mike just discussing, hey, why don't we try this? Yeah, it was just something that we all came up with like, you know, if if we're going to put the onus on the quarterback to have more responsibility, let's practice giving him the freedom to have that responsibility. Um, just to exercise, uh, those things like when you're a quarterback and you're on the ball and you have somebody telling you what to do, it's it's easy to operate. You can kind of tone the thinking down a little bit, uh, so to speak. Uh but when you're in charge of the operation, the communication, getting all of the other 10 guys on the same page, uh but you have no play call, then it's it's pretty cool to see him start to calculate, okay, what is the matchup? Do I think a pressure is coming? Do I have time to get the ball off? What play do I want to get to? Um and so for him to be tuned in, it gives him some ownership of the offense as well. >> And when it concentrates maturation process, considering he has so much control over the pass protection, where does that kind of fall into that program? Um, one more time, please. >> Just in terms of his growth in his second season, better way to say, would you see the protection and his ability to kind of control that? Is that another thing you'd like to see? Maybe take another step. >> Yeah, I think everything that you see uh in terms of the offensive system is something that we're trying to put in Drake's hands and and we have since day one. It's just the consistency of the operation. Um, so as we continue to mature through the system and through the growth of what we're trying to do, I just think you'll see more uh instances of us getting it right, so to speak. >> Yeah. Uh just going back to what AJ was saying last week about how he's you know like stepping up in the meeting rooms as well like interrupting Josh kind of you know sure that's come up but I mean like just can you kind of add some more background on just kind of how he's stepping up like that. >> I think what we're seeing is a is a player who's starting to come into his own in terms of uh his comfort in this building and in this organization and his ownership of the offense. I think the head coach and Josh do a great job of empowering him and giving him those opportunities to speak up. Um, but a lot of that is the study that he puts in and and really the extra meetings and time he spends with Josh to get a a full understanding of exactly what we're trying to do uh with everything in offense in terms of the protection variations in terms of the route concepts uh everything we're doing him and Josh should be in lock step and so when he sees the opportunity to speak up uh in a way that the players can understand it from his perspective I think he's uh going out of his way to do that more often. I think Trayvon did a really good job last year when Mandre had to miss some time and he he stepped in because he was competitive because he worked his butt off because he was working with the mindset of I want to be RB number one. Then when he had an opportunity, he took advantage of it and and he played good football for us and and winning football for us and we were able to uh continue winning uh even though Raandre missed some time. Now, in that room, you know, you have a ton of young guys, kind of Raandre as the vet and then a bunch of younger guys uh in the rest of the room. What have you seen out of Raandre as kind of a leader of that room? He does a great job of sharing his experiences um through the years from when he's talking to the rookies about, hey, this is this is kind of things that happened when I was a rookie and how I dealt with things all the way through when we're watching film and I'm making a correction. He may say, "Hey, Trey, on this I look at this or saw that and this is how this is why I did this." Or it may be when he I'm showing a route or something he did and he may be able to to then I say, "Hey, Raandj, why'd you do that?" And then he can explain to the room why he did something and it may be something that they hadn't thought about or they hadn't experienced and so they do it. Uh and if they can take that and and put that into their toolbox and it helps them, great. >> Um and then just for Jan Miller, I mean, how how has he kind of come along obviously as a rookie? He's doing he's doing a great job. Obviously, um again, he played at a very high level in Alabama, so the physical part is not uh a big jump for him. You know, he's he's he's playing against the same guys he played against in college. Um he's doing a great job thus far working through the mental process of it, and he's he's doing a good job catching on to things. Obviously, it's a little bit more uh probably than what he had been used to in terms of u the system and what he's asked to do as a back in this system. So, he he's he and Miles both are doing a great job of working through it and taking advantage of the opportunities and reps as they get out here at practice. >> What does it take to really, you know, you talk about guys competing for the top spot. What does it take for someone to stand out and say, "Hey, you can be the number one." >> Bet be really good and really consistent. uh because Raandre's done a really good job and he's been consistent. Um and so that's what it takes and you got to bring it every day and he has to bring it every day. But again, understand, know your job, do your job well, know the rules to that allow you to do your job, play with fundamentals and techniques. Obviously, the biggest is is taking care of the football and don't get the quarterback hit. >> Thanks. Who?

title: Drake Maye: "It's Hard Not to Get Excited." | Patriots Press Conference
text: Alrighty. What's going on? >> How are you? >> How you doing? What's up, Karen? >> Great. Um, how are things going for you and AJ Brown? How looks like you're starting to connect fairly uh easily. >> It's hard not to get excited. Um, you know, what a player he is. Um, and just, you know, start off the bat, what a what a great teammate so far. Um, he's eager to learn. Um, he's great with the guys in the locker room and, um, we just look forward to playing with a guy of that caliber and I know he's been a great player in this league. Um he's gone everywhere he's gone. He's been, you know, a guy that you see on on Sports Center the next day, you know, making plays and scoring and um you the best thing about him, he's he's been a winner. You know, he's know what it's like to win and um you have something in that room that you really, you know, kind of we were kind of, you know, kind of looking for and I think that's the best thing. You know, I think Steph provided it for us last year and there's some guys that are growing in the roles, but uh just coming in with that stature and um his ability and his size and just the respect that you walk in there with that kind of Steph had um AJ's got it too. Drake, where are you this year mini campwise now with Drake uh with Josh as far as feeling comfortable with the offense and doing what you do? >> I think it's just naturally night and day from from last year this time. You know, I was trying to, you know, get things right, trying to get guys, you know, know where I was, you know, making making calls and getting guys lined up and now we're just, you know, kind of taking the next steps and that's the best thing about this time. You get to, you know, work on those things and also work on kind of executing and that's the best thing. And coach McDaniels is pushing me hard and he's challenging me and you know trying not to get comfortable during OCTA's and getting comfortable of just doing things and being out here and just making throws. You know, there's a reason and there's a there's a why to it. And that's the best thing about coach McDaniels. He's so good about explaining that why and helping me get to know that why so I can play faster. >> It's a bigger group of receivers overall. What does it do for you as a quarterback to potentially look across the line and have a whole group of bigger targets? >> Yeah, it's it's comforting and you know, no doubt we got guys up there that are um you know, a lot stronger than me in the weight room when I'm dumbbell benching with them. So, um, I think it's it's also something that adds in the run game. You know, it it's it brings kind of physicality to to us to down here in the red zone, you know, makes it easier. Contested catches, you know, really are, you know, they always say 50/50. We're trying to make them that way. And that's when you got guys that can make plays like that. So, you know, I grew up go throwing to my brothers my whole life that are 67 and and tall and big across the middle. So, I'm used to throwing guys at that size. That's awesome. >> You talk about um, you know, the 5050 balls and all that. That's something AJ Brown is known for is being able to get those contested catches. What about his game have you seen in that kind of aspect? And are you excited about having a receiver that you know if you throw that ball, >> he's going to do everything he can to make that happen? >> Yeah, just this really just on me to give him a chance to touch it. Um because more times than not he's going to bring it in. So, um that's exciting. And just knowing that, you know, a slant or something, you know, a quick out, you know, something that you can just give him the ball, he can go and break some tackles and he's tough to tackle and guys don't want to tackle. So, um you know, Romeo brings that, M brings that. you know, we got some guys that are, you know, tougher to tackle than you think and when you get up there and you're guarding them, you're like, man, you know, he can catch a slant and take it the distance. So, um, that's kind of more my mindset to, you know, be on time, you know, make good throws and and let him run with it. >> Obviously, there's a lot of focus on AJ Brown, but Demario Douglas has also been a favorite target of yours in these early practices. What have you seen from him and how has that connection grown between >> since I got here as a rookie, he always just does the right thing. Um, he does the right thing, makes the right plays, um, makes catches. He's hard to cover. Like I said, you can't guard him in a phone booth and he's so good at breaking off in man coverage. Um he's a mismatch, you know, he's so hard to, you know, to to stay in front of and, you know, looking forward to kind of seeing his role kind of, you know, grow bigger. >> Which like you've improved the most >> improve the most? Um I think that's what you're out here doing. You're still trying to improve. You know, it's hard for me to gauge. I'm just kind of just, you know, focused dayto day and, you know, really not, you know, trying to pinpoint an area, you know, trying to get better in all areas. I think it's hard to pinpoint that. I think one thing is just making the right decision. You know, when you know, in the first, you know, few seconds I had the ball in my hand. Making the right decision. Um, knowing that sometimes incompletions are kind of the best plays and not trying to hold the ball too long and kind of get out of the habit of really trying to extend plays just because I feel like I haven't extended a play in a while. >> Drake said earlier that you have a wearability to think ahead, to be ahead a couple of plays. When did you develop this ability to be able to do that and what does it mean to you to be able to do that? I think it's just running plays or being in a formation and just kind of the love for, you know, hey, next time you're in that formation and maybe we can do this. I think whether it's playing Madden or um getting out there at a young age with my dad and being in the formation and throwing a hitch route and you thought the corner jumped in middle school, so next time you run a hitch and go, you know, little things like that where you just pick up on little things and hey, maybe try this and you know, Coach McDaniels was the best in the business at it. So, just trying to learn as much as he can. >> Line of scrimmage maybe been altered this year. Mike was talking about being maybe a little bit more deliberate at the line of scrimmage, taking more ownership. I don't want to misrepresent what he was saying, but just operating at the line of scrimmage. How have you tried to do that? Nicole was wondering too. Spit it out. >> Ashton and Josh were just talking about how they've challenged you at the line and you've gone up to the line of maybe no play call and then it's on you to sort of diagnose what's happening. Just how's that process been going and how do you feel like the feedback? It's kind of trying to be a play caller. You know, it's tough in, you know, this environment when they got 18 seconds on the clock in practice and I'm trying to, you know, do a do a hard count and try and get us in a in a play that we like. So, you know, I think it's awesome for to challenge me and to, you know, push my limits of knowing the offense, knowing what play looks good against what the defense is up. And, um, you know, the best thing that we kind of been trying to focus on is kind of limiting negative plays. you know, negative plays in this league push you behind the chains, whether it's in the red zone, you know, in base downs and just trying to stay ahead of the chains and knowing that, you know, it's really on me to put us in good plays, get us out of bad plays and uh keep the chains, you know, stay ahead of the chains. >> Can you talk a little bit about what this last activity was that you guys were doing on the field with those sleds it looked like team building? Like kind of talk us through what >> we split up into teams. Um, you know, split up in the families at the beginning of the offseason. Uh, kind of had about, you know, 13 teams, you know, had some captains in each team. Um, and some some different guys and has about seven players in each. We kind of been keeping a point tally. Um, you know, kind of how we've been doing with the families. You know, I think my family's maybe in second, so we got some work to do to get that, you know, kind of final first first place push. But yeah, the lowest time to come out here and push some sleds and try to compete against each other and uh just another way of team building and um, you know, competing and having to strategize and, you know, kind of have something that may not go right and try to fix it. >> What does What does the winning team get? >> Say that one time. >> What does the winning team get? >> Yeah, we asked that. We asked that in leadership group. Uh, coach, I think Frabel's kind of coming up with something. So, hopefully something pretty good over the course of your career going up against a guy like Carl Davis. >> Say it one more time. >> What's it meant to you over the course of last year, plus going up against a guy like Carl Davis on a regular basis? >> Man, CD has been awesome. Uh, he's awesome in the locker room. We get out there before practice, he's saying, "Hey, throw throw throw one at me and and come challenge me today." So, you know, he wants work and he's proven in this league as a a guy to make plays on the football. um you know he's one of the best at you know being physical being on his man and man coverage and you know he's a winner you know he's won it and he knows what it's like to win and obviously done a lot of things right in his career so it's awesome to have you know him and Gonzo and you know even some more corners and DBs you know that backend group that they got over there it was a real tough challenge for us and um you know us receivers so it's it's been awesome and CD is just he's always in a great mood and um he's he's fun to be out here with >> there I know that was the last one but >> yeah always

title: Josh McDaniels: "You Can Just See the Growth of the Group." | Patriots Press Conference
text: Is she getting a big party and everything? >> Hey, that's Laura. >> Josh, what have you seen maybe a year ago to now as far as coming into these types of things with what you're able to do? >> Pleasure. >> Um, well, I mentioned it last week, you know, about Drake, but I think it probably holds true to most of the group. um you know there was only a couple guys that had ever been um in our language in our system um prior to last season. So um I think like anything you know it's your second year doing something uh more comfort level across the board. Um, I think guys know the the words, uh, what they mean to them, uh, how to use it, uh, to their benefit and you can just see, I think, the the growth of the group together and and, um, yeah, it just, it just seems like we're, you know, we should be, I mean, that's the reality is is when you return a good portion of guys and you have have some continuity on the staff and on the team, um, you should have an opportunity to feel better, uh, execute better, and and hopefully improve across the board. So, um, they're working really hard at it. I know that the attitude's been great, and, uh, I'm looking forward to finishing up the spring and head into the summer. >> Josh, you've worked with a lot of a lot of quarterbacks in your career. Where does Drake stand in terms of his ability to absorb and grow with the information that you give him in terms of taking it to the field? Um he's he's pretty good, you know. He's pretty good. Um he's really smart and uh and he works hard at it. Um you know, I said this last year, he asks he asks a lot of really good questions because he's thinking ahead. Um the game makes sense to Drake. Um, that's probably, I'd say, comes a lot from his father, you know, and just having a chance to grow up in that kind of a uh a household and and have those conversations. But, um, yeah, he's he's a he's a quick processor. He's a quick study. Uh, he learns and takes things to the field pretty quickly. >> And you mentioned you mentioned something. How rare is it to be able to think ahead of >> Yeah, it's a benefit. Um, you know, and because I think part of our game, whether we like it or not, is sometimes it's the hardest part for us is, you know, you you put a game plan together or you're doing something, but you have to see some of the obstacles that aren't necessarily right in front of you. Um, in order to do that, you got to think a couple steps ahead. So, um, yeah, he's he's still a young player, but I'd say he's he's really at an accelerated rate when it comes to his processing. before coaches, you know, they just have sort of memory just over a calendar year now. Have you noticed that? >> Yeah, it's pretty good. Um it doesn't I don't nothing surprises me with him anymore. Uh because he's that's kind of how it's been since I've met him. Um he's got great recall. um he you know some of us I don't know how many in this gaggle of people uh may or may not had to take a bunch of notes in college or as we were learning um I don't know how many notes he has to take you know he's a processor while you're talking about it you know what I mean he does he takes notes but um he processes through through the conversation and he can see the game as you're talking about it which is cool um because what everybody, you know, there's this part, but then there's also that part on game day where we can't go into the meeting room, watch the film, put it on a whiteboard, you know, it's verbal. It's all verbal, you know, other than maybe seeing a little something on the tablet. So, um, it gives you an opportunity to make some quick adjustments and corrections, but his memory is really good. What to optimal wide receiver quarter? >> I think any I mean the receivers want to get open and catch the ball and the quarterback wants to get it to him. Um I think that's the simple part. Um I think the working together and the understanding one another and what uh what one's capable of and and what the other one wants. you know, when the quarterback is looking for something to make him comfortable and the receiver thinks he can do this. Um, I think it just there's a dynamic there. Uh, it's fun to go through the process of building that, especially with two very talented players. Um, I I would say that that's probably the case for our entire skill group, though. Um, they're all doing that right now. They take reps with each other. Sometimes it's the first rep they've had at something, sometimes it's the seventh or 10th or whatever, and you can just see the growth as they do it. So, more repetitions, build great habits. Uh that's what we're out here trying to do and I think those two are are hard at work at trying to do the same thing. >> You didn't have the group together very long, but does the you have this year wide receiver remind you at all that 2019 group with Julian Edelman and Josh Gordon and Antonio Brown. How do you go about managing a room with so many talented? >> I don't know if it reminds me of any group. Um but you know, I mean there's a lot of guys that can do a lot of um interesting things. Um, you know, the the good thing is is really there's not I don't know that there's two guys that are really, you know, close to being the same. They all offer different things, different abilities, different skill sets. Um, our job is just to try to figure out how to put them out there and let them have an opportunity to do those things as much as we can. There's other two there's two other skill groups that are involved in that conversation, too, with the tight ends and uh and the backs. And you guys have seen those guys, too. So, um, you know, it's, look, it's fun. Uh, this time of the year is really good because you, everybody gets an opportunity to rep and learn and make mistakes and then correct it and then learn from it and get better. So, that's what we're trying to do. And, uh, you know, at the end of August, as we head into the regular season, hopefully we figured out the best way to do it with the group. >> Learned about AJ in the short time. >> Very smart. um really um enjoys the game of football and and I you could just tell that he's had um a great deal of experience at a high level, you know, um whether that's route technique, understanding coverage, releases, top of the routes, um how to do certain things, you know, on in situational football, whatever it might be. Uh he's certainly had uh a great deal of highle experience. Uh you can feel that when you talk to him. Um, but he's also really intelligent, understands the game, his position, uh, what it takes to be successful. So, it's been it's been awesome. I'm I'm excited we have him. Uh, looking forward to continuing to build our relationship, uh, and continuing to get him, you know, acclimated to our to our offense. >> Josh, Mike said yesterday that you and Ashton were working with Drake on limiting mistakes at the line of scrimmage. How have you seen progress there? Yeah, I think I think that's much the same as what we talked about with everything else that he's doing. You know, he's further ahead in that regard. Um, you know, there's nothing worse for an offense than ne negative plays. Um, they kind of they put you in bad situations and uh we we saw that last year, you know, when when that happened to us, you know, it's it's hard to overcome those things. I don't care who you are. Um, so, uh, you know, we're just we're trying to to do what we can, um, at each position, not just at quarterback, but certainly he has a say in all of those. Um, and so I think his comfort level, I think his maturity and understanding of how bad those things are for the offense. I think that's, um, that's taken a huge step forward. He understands it. He gets it. And so, um, through that, uh, hopefully we'll be much improved in that area, uh, when we get to the regular season. >> Two more questions. AJ, >> when we were talking to you last week, you made the the one for one comparison, but the physical Bronco like maybe the closest thing. When you look at that, >> do you put it on yourself like I got to hunt mismatches for this guy because of the size and strength? I know you're early in the process, but is that something that goes through your brain when it comes to AJ? it depends. Um, you know, it depends on what kind of defense you're talking about. Is it a team that plays a lot of man-to-man zone? Um, you know, who are the corners? You know, how do they play? Um, you know, I'm sure he'd probably be the first one to tell you that he's he is a mismatch. So, um I'm not sure how how long I have to hunt for them, but um but but I understand the level of of player the the scheme uh how they try to take, you know, players away or or at least limit them. Uh that impacts all of our decisions every week and how we go about trying to create the best offensive performance for our team. So, um I I think all of that stuff honestly will kind of play out in as as we go. I think right now the biggest thing for us is, you know, learning multiple positions, being able to handle moving around, understanding what we're doing, how does it work with the quarterback. Um, getting acclimated in that regard so that we're able to do those things if and when we need to, you know. So, um, but I don't think that process is going to take long. Uh, he's very quick learner and, um, like I said, he's a he's a true pro. >> Last question, >> Josh, how do you feel in those situations yesterday? you kind of hurry to the line but then in a hurry to snap it. >> Yeah. >> Um, you know, does he have some freedom there to maybe decide what to do in those moments? How did he >> Yeah, I think I think he's getting I mean I hope he's getting better at everything and that's one of them. Uh, Phil, um, you know, like the quarterback at the line of scrimmage, you have you can do two things. You can tell them that they don't have much freedom and responsibility and just tell them to snap the football and hope for the best and try to execute as best they can. Uh or you can if they're capable and able and willing and want to and can do it at a high level, you can give them uh some tools um for them to try to use to help us in every way, whether that's get out of a bad one, run a good one, whatever, you know. And I think Drake's uh clearly capable of of helping the football team in multiple situations like that. Um I think he's definitely making progress in that area. Um I think his overall command and leadership in general is taking a big step forward. Um really uh really happy with his progress in that regard. >> All right, guys. >> Okay. Thank you.

title: Mike Vrabel: "We Have to Play With a Certain Speed." | Patriots Press Conference
text: Hey guys. >> Hello. >> How are you? >> Good. You >> great. Got here late. Karen in the second row. >> Yes, I was. >> Um >> I know it's early. Uh but what have you seen from the Drake and AJ connection? >> Well, I mean, again, I I think that um you know, they found each other a couple times yesterday in the red zone. Um and I think that's a work in progress. I think that's just how it goes from from having um you know a player come in that you know I think that connection is critical to to rely on you know a quarterback or receiver have to be on the same page. you know, practice is critical, the reps are critical, they're, you know, I think sometimes when you get players that have had success in this league and they come, you know, onto your team, you know, you get an opportunity to to learn maybe what's worked for them and what they've uh been able to, you know, pick up over the years of of doing it. And so, there's some professional initiative. I think we have we have that in every um facet of our of our program when the players go out there whether it's you know Kevin Bard or you know Draymond Jones is say you know can we do it this way yeah sure as long as we're on the same page and you know so I think that'll happen with with Drake and AJ as well that there'll be some things that you know maybe he's done before that he likes and you know there'll be things that that we'll add new to him. How much does it help, Mike, in year two with you, the staff, and the and many of the players returning for a mini camp like this? >> Uh, well, we've what you guys have seen is really what we've done. It's just a little bit, you know, maybe a few extra maybe an hour and a half longer uh day. So, but that that's what a normal OTAA looks like, you know, an OTAA practice. It's just, you know, we've got to get them out of here um you know, in a certain time. And so we have a little bit more time in in for meetings and you know our walkth through. Um but that's kind of what it's looked like and I think that that's you know to your point it's probably looked better uh in the spring. You know that doesn't mean a whole lot other than that maybe that they understand how we need to practice or how what we want to do and how we you know the urgency and tempo in which we practice and all those habits that we try to create that are positive. Now, uh to that point, today will probably look a little different. Um probably won't be as much speed stuff. Uh but we'll come back and and get that same uh speed that we had yesterday uh further down in the red zone uh tomorrow. So, it'll it'll look a little different today just by design as far as the pace that you'll see, but I you know, I guess to your point, I was happy with whatever pace we had had yesterday. >> With Morgan Moses, I'm just curious. We saw him leave Otis early last week and then wasn't out there yesterday. Is he dealing with an injury or is this more of like kind of veteran rest? Like what's kind of going on? >> Yeah, it was just managing and Morgan and and excited that he's, you know, so committed to our football team and the and the people here. Um, you know, just a a positive addition last year and, you know, he'll have a plan through training camp. It's a long season. You know, he was important to us. It'll be very important to us going forward. So, you know, just trying to make sure that we manage manage him and, you know, figure every every rep now is is probably one less that he may take uh in the season. So, want to try to get him to a point where, you know, he's ready to go, give each guy exactly what they need and, you know, everybody will have a plan. >> How is um adjusted to being on the right side? >> Um I, you know, I think that he again, he's getting a lot of reps. I love the versatility. I think when you get a young player, um, there the willingness to to learn and just kind of adapt and adjust. There hasn't been, you know, oh my gosh, I'm so used to this. I I think it's all new to him. So, you know, his flexibility and versatility has been something that um, you know, I I think has has stood out. Uh, learns quickly, usually doesn't make the same mistake twice. Uh, and it is different, you know. So the guys that you're trying to put in different places and say you got to get as much reps on on the left as you do on the right. Uh that's that's important. And so he's done a done a nice job of that. >> Mike, you know, for as a player and a coach, how important the mental aspect of this game is. How good is this group now in it second year of absorbing what you teach them in the classroom and translating it to what they do on the field? >> Well, I mean, I think there's always going to be mistakes. I think our job is to is to coach and and uh correct mistakes and and find ways to to teach them. You know, the the the things that you that are non-negotiable are just uh you know, the way that we play and our style and our the conditioning and you know, our our ability to to finish consistently um when you when you do make a mistake and some of the most instinctive players that I've been around have been able to do that. they've been able to to make a mistake early on in the play formationally, but but get it fixed, get it adjusted, you know, run the wrong route, block the wrong guy, but still find a way to to salvage the play. So, those are the things that we're working on. You know, we can we can coach mistakes, uh, and we can correct them. We just can't, you know, make too many of the same mistakes. Mike, would you like to add at tight end after Julian's injury or is >> I think that's just from a number standpoint in camp. I think that's somewhere we'll probably have to, you know, evaluate the numbers. You know, there's 90 guys, 91 guys on every team. So, um, yeah, we'll just have to, you know, take a look at that. But I would say that that's probably somewhere where, you know, we would have to address. >> What have been your impressions of Eli Ridan so far? uh willing, conscientious, wants to learn. I think there's a lot of new things that coming from, you know, college and, you know, terminology is different and there's a lot of things that are new to him. But I would say that he picks things up quickly and uh you know, when he's able to to play with the speed that, you know, he has available to him in his body, that's kind of showed out. Um, and then with a lot of these young guys, just the terminology, the routes, the coverage, just try to eliminate and allow them to to play as fast as possible. So, in the spring, it's like, hey, let's try to play out of control. Let's play too fast. And then if you make a mistake, like that's fine, but we got to start training that play speed so that when we do grasp everything um really well, you know, he the play speed is there. you know, that's not something that I we should learn what to do and to go slow. We we have to play at a play speed that we're going to need in the games and the ability to to separate or get open. And so, that's just been a focus that we've tried to ask him to do is is as you learn is is play a little faster and if you make mistakes, we'll we'll coach them, but but we have to play with a certain speed. >> What have you seen from Carlton Davis going into his second year with you guys? >> Well, MCD is a great teammate. He's a competitive player. um as you continue to um gain years in this league, you know, you have to continue to find, especially at those speed positions, you have to find some different pitches. You have to find, you know, some minor adjustments and tweaks. And um I know that he's continuing to focus on that and do that, but he was a competitive player. He's a competitive person. Um and excited to, you know, have him back. How do you envision Shane Bowen contributing to the staff? >> Well, Shane's got a lot of experience in how we do things. He's been very valuable to to me personally going back to to Houston. Um or you know, excuse me, going back to Ohio State and uh you know, we learned how to coach together and that's the thing I'll always uh appreciate about Shane is that we we we learned how to coach and I'm proud of what he's done in this league and excited about him and being here and helping us. just ex assist the defense and help some of the young guys. Excited about Kevin Richardson and and BJ Edmonds who's, you know, those are younger coaches on our staff that those guys can can go to Shane and ask him and rely on him to, you know, fill in the gaps maybe why some of the other coaches, you know, have something going on or they're meeting with players. Uh but I think just having a you know another guy that's called plays in this league and is game planned and uh we'll be able to provide assistance to to offensively and you know but I think it'll help us. >> Mike, understanding the attention and maybe gravity that AJ brings at receiver. How much of the playbook would has been adjusted for that since he got here? >> Uh I I think we're probably a little early for that. I think that the adjustments are can can come. It's been a couple you know. I mean, it's been maybe a week. So, I think it's learning what we do the formations. There's so many different formations, personnel groups. I think we have to get that down first before we start, you know, going on to adjustments and, you know, what are we going to do? But that that'll all be part of it. >> In the wide receiver room, you also have a lot of young wide receivers and a lot of uh some UDFAs you signed this season. What are you looking for these practices to maybe earn a spot on the roster? what more could they contribute if it's, you know, >> well, I mean, it's always, you know, being ready for your opportunity, but again, watching and seeing, uh, Kyle's development and, you know, Chis taking advantage of his opportunities and, you know, that's just one position and then being able to add the guys that we did in the postdraft. Um, like I told him yesterday, when we have those different periods and they get extra reps that they have to have to take advantage of them, you know, when you do a good job and a nice job, you get more opportunity. the more positions that you know I think certainly would help them and if they don't then they just have to learn the ones that they can. Um but you just never know in a preseason game or practice or a scrimmage uh when that opportunity is going to come um just like Chis maybe last year in some of those preseason games and and what he was able to do. So you know we try to give them the blueprint and uh you know then they can make make what uh they can. Mike, would you guys ever consider bringing digs back? >> I mean, I think we've, you know, probably at the number that we would need right now. I wouldn't say anything is off the table. We would want to add anybody that could help us. I not going to give a percentage on it, but I think we're we're we're happy with where we're at right now uh with the numbers and the people in the receiver room. You know, I appreciate uh Stfan as as a person and as a player and what he did for us last year. I'll value that. um helped us win football games, helped us, you know, get to where we got. Uh but right now, I I don't think that that's something that, you know, I think we're we're exploring, but I would never say no. >> Uh yesterday, yesterday you said like a defense side springs the time to test different like fleas, disguise before paring things down. Uh what usually like determines a defensive like a new idea that survive into the training camp is that player feed, execution, communication or some other things? >> Well, I think it go it's it's a it's everything. It's how it fits and what the players can understand. That's the most important thing. What they're comfortable with, what they um what they show you on the field and and their ability to to handle it, to understand it. You don't want to get too cute when when this game is not about getting cute. It's about having answers and and try and doing some new things and enhancing some things, but but we don't want to get, you know, cute when you add ideas, whether that's offensively or defensively or on special teams. So, I think you start by what the players can handle and, you know, take a look at it and see how it gets tested over the course of the spring like we talked about or, you know, when you get to training camp and, you know, you're starting to see more, you know, closer to live action. to AJ Brown >> one more time. Uh, since last time you worked with him, is there anything that's kind of surprised you that he's added to his game or tweaked at all or has it kind of been same old same old with age? >> I mean, I think there's still savvy that, you know, has improved and, you know, was a younger player uh when we were together. Um, you know, that continued to develop and and get and improve. um you know so I don't I mean maybe there's a little bit of savvy but I think he's showed up with a great attitude and and really um you know I've enjoyed watching his interactions with the other players on the team. I think that's probably the thing that I'm most excited about right now. >> Mike, what's the biggest difference you've seen uh in Elijah Ponder from the Super Bowl to the guy you're working with now? >> I think maybe confidence of you know I'm actually here. title: Drake Maye's "new tools" and a major focus at Patriots minicamp Day 2
text: All right, 2 minutes from day two of Patriots mini camp here, a walk-through, a jog-through at times, but nothing really competitive. This was a slow practice that the Patriots held entirely inside the red zone. You're not going to have any Drake Maye stats. We're not going to tell you about any highlight plays from A.J. Brown, but we will get into some details and then two bigger picture points of what I think the emphasis so far in mini camp has told us here about what this team wants to do next season, of course, win, but how they're going to do it. Starting though with those details. Chris Hogan Dallas, full participant. Sounds pretty good, right? Again, the only periods he's missed through two days have been live competitive 11-on-11s. When those periods are at a higher injury risk than anything else that they're doing. If it's a walk-through, if it's a jog-through, if it's an individual drill, he's there, but when they go full speed and full team, he's been sitting out. Caleb Lomu started again at right tackle, worked in again at left tackle as Will Campbell's primary backup, another indicator that the Patriots ideally would have him as their swing tackle this year, but as long as Morgan Moses sits out, which the plan is for him to sit out the remainder of spring, meaning basically tomorrow, uh Caleb Lomu, the first-round rookie, will be there at right tackle. Speaking of Moses being out, he again was joined by Harold Landry and Gabe Ikard on the sideline. Ikard's really on the sideline of this entire affair because he's just not here. Uh but Harold Landry not expected to participate again as he recovers from off-season knee surgery. So, um what were those two big points of emphasis that the Patriots are putting on this mini camp? Well, number one pertains to Drake Maye, and this is his ability to handle responsibilities at the line of scrimmage and pre-snap. This is something Mike Vrabel talked about before practice on Tuesday saying, "He's really been challenged," meaning Drake, "by Josh McDaniels and Astor Grant, the quarterbacks coach, to get more often into the right play and sift through defensive disguises." And look, he's going into year three as a quarterback. This is a part of the natural learning curve and life of a young quarterback, but when you look back at the Super Bowl, what gave him bigger problems than anything else? It was the Seahawks pressure and the inability to have solutions for that pressure. So, today, before practice, I spoke with Ashton Grant, again, his quarterbacks coach, and said, "What has that been like challenging him at the line of scrimmage?" And Ashton Grant said they've given him, quote, "new tools," end quote, meaning both things that were in the playbook but not accessible to Drake last year cuz you don't want to drink from a fire hose as a second-year quarterback who's in his first year of a system, and new things they've added to the offense to help give him answers to do different defensive problems. So, there's that part. They put that into action, not today, but yesterday when Drake May, as Ashton Grant told us, would run to the line in those live 11-on-11 periods and didn't have a play call. His job was to get everyone organized in information and then read the defense and make the call for himself. This way, the coaching staff could identify A, whether he saw the defense correctly, and then B, got into the right play. And when they went to review those plays from yesterday in the meetings afterward, uh quote, "I think he did very well." That was Ashton Grant. Now, the second piece about this about the what the Patriots were trying to solve is red zone work. They have spent virtually all of minicamp inside the red zone. And when you go back and look at the numbers or listen to our old podcast, the defense was among the worst, if not the worst, for long stretches of last season inside the 20-yard line. The offense wasn't much better, and part of that had to do with their inability to run in short yardage and in tight quarters and high-leverage situations. But for now, the fact the Patriots have spent so much time there, even with added weapons, another problem they tried to solve with Romeo Dobbs and A.J. Brown, they have put an emphasis on we have to be better inside the 20 to convert those field goals into touchdowns or stop allowing touchdowns and force more field goals. The last thing I'll add is this. Uh practice did not end with football. It ended with sled races as the Patriots were split up into different teams of six players from all different positions, all different ages. These are their quote, "families" this offseason as the coaches have organized different competitions, including a scavenger hunt earlier this spring. And based on how you finish in the scavenger hunt or the sled race, your family gets to number of points. We had Elliott Wolf out here with a stopwatch, Ryan Cowden. So, you had regular staffers, front office executives, everyone watching, pushing a sled, timing, cheering, etc. as a way to continue to build camaraderie, something that was very successful last year and clearly is a point of emphasis this offseason. title: Giants Assistant Coaches Speak From Minicamp | New York Giants
text: Just is Josh a guy that can play all the positions or or you guys see him as a tackle? >> No, Josh has position flex. Yeah, I think guard and tackle is very possible. Uh we've tried to leave him at tackle as much as possible through this offseason program and that's where we're planning to start him in training camp. >> Thank you. Hey Paul Schwarz with the New York Post. >> Hey Paul, nice to meet you. >> Same year. Um so did you run up the card at number 10? That was your that was your >> I didn't get the opportunity to run it up but I can tell you nobody in the building could have been more excited than I was. And I think the thing that maybe allowed him to stand out more in the process for me was the fact that he's been coached by Alex Mirbball at Miami and nobody is doing better in college football than Alex. His group, the way he teaches uh their foundational knowledge of this game, it's just next level. So, it's almost like, yes, he's a rookie. Of course, he's a rookie. And you know, you're always scared to death with with freshman freshman in college and rookies in the NFL. It's like the old scary movies, right? Like you tell her not to go around a corner, she still does. And there's going to be some incidents like that. And there have been at practice where as a rookie, you know, even though you told him, sometimes you have to live that moment. And uh but the thing Cece is doing a great job of is not making the same mistake twice. >> How you you came in, you know, there's four starters, you know, no nothing's guaranteed, but there are four guys lining up who were starters last year in their same positions. So now you come in as a new offensive line coach. How has that dynamic been? You know, they they did it one way. They were, you know, a better offensive line last year than they have been in years. And now you come in and it's like got a rookie, of course. You don't change everything, but you got to change something. You're the their coach now. How has that been? >> Yeah, you're changing a system. So everybody understands that. Like, you know, it's it's part of this deal. And if you don't win enough games, systems change, people change. And that's what happened. I think they've all attacked it like pros. And I've enjoyed coming to work with them every single day. their mindset, their desire to learn and to want more information about the system. It's been so much fun. Now, I do think Karm did a great job with this room. I think there was great foundational knowledge in there. I got a lot of respect for Karm. And so, it's again, we're teaching a new system. We're teaching new things to call and and new techniques, but so much of it is just being able to assimilate back to what they did. And that gives us a great baseline to start from. >> Thank you very much. >> Absolutely. >> How would you advise CC on on switching from tackle to guard? I think everyone's kind of talked to him about it, but how would you how do you advise him on how to adjust well to that? >> You know, the thing that that happens faster is everything at guard. That's the bottom line. You know, when you're at tackle and you've got an edge rusher, you've got time and space to work with and and some people that's going to be harder for, some people it's going to be easier for. When you move a guy like that that's only played tackle in games, it's getting the speed of pass protection, the speed of the games, and the speed at which those twists happen. That's the biggest thing. And so again, time on task, repetition is the mother of all learning. And how many reps can we get to get you so comfortable? The nice thing is he did take guard reps. He did take center reps at Miami in practice. So it's not his first rodeo, but obviously this is a pretty big stage for it. And they people said he seems natural. I think Jackson say he seems natural. Have you been surprised at how he's been able to kind of transition a little bit from that experience? You know, >> uh, I guess he I was very hopeful the transition would look like this, but it has been very smooth. Did you study him like after you got this job and look back and say, "Okay, let me see how he struggled and why it didn't work together and you know have any theories behind that?" >> Well, we studied every player. You know, we try to look at every player. We make these tapes called get better tapes and there things we need to get better at. And we try to just show him his consistency was his deal. He just wasn't consistent getting lined up fast. Wasn't consistent with his feet. So, he's improved his consistency. Now, his play is improved and now his confidence is up and he can keep this rolling into the season. talking about Deontay Banks it sounds like. Yes. So in reference to Paulson Adivbo when you looked at where he was at last year and looked at that film where did you think he needed to get better? >> Well I think Pollson had the same thing. He just needed to be more consistent. That's the overarching theme I thought throughout the whole secondary. We just be need to be consistent with our techniques, consistent with our alignments where our eyes are and then not over complicate this game. The game's already hard enough. So for us to throw more complication in it, it's crazy. make it simple for those guys so they can play fast and those skills their mama and daddy gave them show up. >> This is do would you say this is a simpler backend scheme than what they were doing last year? >> I don't think anything's simple in the in the in the NFL. You know what I'm saying? You have to be multiple enough to be able to work against these great offensive coordinators and quarterbacks that you face. He's going to come in here compete for a starting job. So, where is he in that right now and how would you assess his development? >> He's doing a great job for us. He's intelligent. He looks like he belongs. All the skill sets there. So, it's going to be good. How do you approach a guy like Tay who >> has had some struggles, you know, his first few years in the league just in terms of of getting to know him and and helping him go forward from here? >> Well, that's my whole coaching style. I really pour into these guys. I want to have a good relationship because relationships makes him be able to trust me. And if he can trust me, he's going to do what I say more often. So, right now, we've built the trust and he's being consistent in his technique. So that's all we really needed from him to prove that he can do and now he's showing up day in and day out. He's being a pro. He's putting in extra work. So he's motivated to do the right things and he's headed in the right direction. >> With Colton, much has been made obviously about he's got great jeans. His uncle played for for coach Harbaugh. I'm just curious, do you see kind of that technique and learning from him already that he's been well taught by obviously his uncle and what he's learned so far? >> Yes, he's picked up the techniques very fast for a young rookie coming in this deal. He's settled into what we're trying to get accomplished with the scheme and as far as our technique and he's doing a good job applying those skills. Now it's just some of the stuff when we get down the field that's in flight is, hey, we need to stay on top leverage. We don't need to undercut some things and it's the little things that he's going to get and get more consistent with and then you're going to be able to see him take off and play well. >> But it's a good foundation you think already from what he's learned. >> Incredible foundation. Those guys have taught him well. They did a great job with him at his past schools. His uncle has clearly done a good job with him. So, his transition has been faster than a lot of guys would be >> or is this a different place, but is is he still the same still the same system? >> Um, same guy. >> Uh, he's he's John, you know, but um he's he's got a lot of energy. Um, I think it's just a hard ball thing. You know, started with Jack and Jackie. Um, and and and Jim and Joanie. I just think it's a hard ball thing. When I and what I mean by that, uh, when it comes to coaching, I think for the most part, you either get one or the other when it comes to force for forcefulness or sincerity. And not many coaches have both. And when you're dealing with the Harball, they they have them both. They know how to do them both and do them very well. And, um, they're great with people. And um and as a player, you you appreciate that. You appreciate when a coach can get on you and and also when a coach can uh pat you on the bat and tell you did a good job as well. >> He's kind of straddling the line between players coach and disciplined guy. Not necessarily either one. >> Well, I I wouldn't say it's a player coach or anything. He's just he's just he's a good damn football coach, you know what I mean? that can that can really um motivate um people, motivate players and and and and but also teach them and how to do things, you know, and and and you get it what you get from what you get from John is is is realness. What was it like for the early stages of putting this offense together with all you guys in a room and everybody's different ideas? You know, um, considering like you say, we have a lot of football minds in there, a lot of guys been head coaches or coordinators and things of that nature. Do >> you have an idea yet of what this is going to look like when you roll it out in September?
